title: Making Sense of Self Doubt: "What if I Am Wrong?"
author: The Silent Struggle
summary: The Silent Struggle opens with a personal account of staying silent in a high-stakes meeting out of fear of being wrong, then generalizes it into a broader argument about what leadership actually is: not the possession of a pre-existing right answer, but the willingness to offer an interpretation before anyone else has articulated one. Drawing on organizational researcher Karl Weick, the piece reframes 'sense-making' as leadership's real, underdiscussed function — making coherent sense of the past, the messy present, and an uncertain future for the people around you. Its central psychological insight, also from Weick, is that certainty typically follows speech rather than preceding it ('you don't know what you think until you see what you said'), which inverts the common workplace assumption that credibility requires certainty before speaking. The piece closes with Weick's parable of three baseball umpires — 'I call them as they are,' 'I call them as I see them,' and 'they ain't nothing till I call them' — to argue that most consequential leadership moments are closer to the third umpire's stance: nothing is decided until someone decides it, so waiting for objective certainty before speaking up is often waiting for something that will never arrive.
points: The article's core reframe of leadership — 'leadership rarely means seeing the truth before everyone else does; more often it means being willing to offer an interpretation that wasn't articulated yet' — directly counters the common assumption that leaders must be right before they speak.

Karl Weick's claim that 'you don't know what you think until you see what you said' inverts the usual sequence of certainty-then-speech, suggesting that withholding a half-formed idea until it feels certain may itself be a barrier to developing the idea.

The three-umpires parable gives a memorable, reusable framework: most workplace moments requiring a leadership read are closer to 'they ain't nothing till I call them' than to 'I call them as they are' — meaning waiting for objective certainty is often waiting for something that doesn't exist.

The organizational example (mid-management looking up for the answer, senior leadership looking down for signals, departments pointing at each other) illustrates how an entire organization can collectively stall by assuming the right answer exists in someone else's office.
quotes: What if I'm wrong, and everyone in the room can see it except me?" I remember sitting in a meeting room, there were too many people I didn't know well and few senior people for me to be comfortable.
The conversation moved on without me making a point, and I felt disappointment and relief at the same time.
Everyone, somewhere in the org chart, is convinced the right answer is sitting in someone else's office.
Leadership rarely means seeing the truth before everyone else does. More often it means being willing to offer an interpretation that wasn't articulated yet.

The organisational researcher Karl Weick suggests you don't know what you think until you see what you said. Certainty isn't reliably the thing that comes before you speak, it shows up after we speak, or it could not show up at all.
The first says, "I call them as they are". He believes there's an objective, measurable truth out there, and his job is simply to register it.

Most of us move through work assuming we're the first umpire, waiting to register a truth that already exists, if only we look hard enough or wait long enough. But most of the moments that matter at work, the ones where people are looking to you for a read, are closer to the third. Nothing is decided until someone decides it.
